headline: Approved $43,500,000 bond for Public Works garage, $5,000,000 for two pools, and $11,692,041.56 wastewater plant contract.
summary: An ordinance letting people with disabilities comment remotely at full meetings passed 10-3. A $2,000,000 Four Hills Landfill bond was tabled, and a $5,173,428 equipment bond went back to Budget Review. The mayor said state school aid will be a little more than $4 million less than last year.
decisions: Accepted and placed on file the report on energy contract savings and cost avoidance.
Accepted and placed on file the communication on disposition of 342 Main Street.
Approved a contract for replacement copiers, not to exceed $35,220 with Toshiba Financial Services, 60 monthly payments.
Approved a 36-month extension of the city's primary internet service with Fidium Enterprise Services, not to exceed $29,484.
Approved a three-year Microsoft Software Assurance contract with SHI International, not to exceed $68,310.08.
Approved a construction contract with Loureiro Building Construction for the wastewater plant Phase I upgrade, not to exceed $11,692,041.56, contingent on additional bond funding. Johnson opposed.
Approved a contract with Wright Pierce for construction administration on the wastewater Phase I upgrade, not to exceed $1,361,000.
Approved a $3,597 change order for the Renaissance Park audio system. Johnson opposed.

Sent R-26-064, as amended, back to Budget Review Committee, with a public hearing set for October 26.
Adopted Ordinance O-26-002, allowing electronic public comment for people with disabilities, as amended, 10-3.
Referred R-26-075, the second amended federal aid agreement for Taylor Falls and Veterans bridges with an additional $231,941.29, to the Finance Committee.

A regular meeting of the Board of Aldermen was held Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at 7:30 p.m. in the alderma nic 
chamber, and duly noticed in two places, including the City’s website, in accordance with the requirem ents of RSA 91-
A:2 II. 
  
President Lori Wilshire presided; City Clerk Dan Healey recorded. 
 
Prayer was offered by City Clerk Dan Healey; Alderwoman Vengerflutta Smith led in the Pledge to the Flag.  
 
Let’s start the meeting by taking a roll call attendance.  
 
The roll call was taken with 13 members of the Board of Aldermen present:  Alderman Clemons, Alderman Klee, 
Alderman Ravan, Alderwoman Smith, Alderman Thibeaul t, Alderman O’Brien, Alderman Gregg, Alderman Dowd, 
Alderman Sullivan, Alderman Sennott, Alderman Johns on, Alderman Morgan, Alderman Wilshire.    
     
Alderwoman Kelly and Alderman Lopez were recorded a bsent.   
 
President Wilshire 
 
I did hear from Alderwoman Kelly that she had a sick child so she will not join us this evening. 
 
Mayor James W. Donchess and Corporation Counsel Ste ve Bolton were also in attendance. 
 
REMARKS BY THE MAYOR  
 
Mayor Donchess 
 
Yes, Madam President, I had a few items.  First of all, I wanted to direct the attention of the Board of Aldermen to the 
memo which came from Amy Girard and is number one o n the Communications.  It outlines how the City has saved 
about or will save about $600,000 in total as a result of locking in lower than market - current marke t rates for fuel and 
also electricity.  Most of the savings come from th e electric savings, but that has to do with the power that is being 
purchased at much less than the Eversource rate of about 14 cents per kilowatt hour.  So I'd like to certainly thank Amy 
Girard and everyone involved here.  I'm sure Doria Brown was involved as well in achieving these saving s for the 
taxpayers of the City of Nashua.  
 
Next Madam President, I wanted to mention that an item on the agenda tonight is the - there are a number  of bond 
issues on the agenda but one of them - the largest one - is for the completion of the Public Works garage project which 
was begun with Phase 1.  That was the construction of the office which exists out at the landfill now.  We have also, of 
course, borrowed and invested money in designing the project.  But the garage that we have was built in the 1970s on - 
I'm going to say on the cheap.  It has out used its life.  It has extended beyond its real life and is in such bad shape now 
that the garage needs to be replaced for the benefit of the Public Works employees and the functions o f Public Works 
which touch our residents every single day and I see we have a number of our Public Works employees an d Paul Shea, 
a Commissioner, here tonight I assume in support of that project, which is very much needed.  
 
Madam President, I did want to inform the Board of s ome bad news which we got from the State of New Ham pshire 
which is that we've been - we've learned that the school aid that the City will receive is going to be a little more than $4 
million less than in the prior fiscal year.  In proposing the budget, we had assumed a $2 million decr ease but it turns out 
it's going to be 4.5 approximately.  This is very unfortunate.  It reflects, I believe, a lack of support at the State level for 
our New Hampshire's children.  People have said, and I think it's correctly said, that a public education system is the 
basis of the American dream and why is that true?  Because that is how kids that don't have a lot of me ans, who don't 
have parents who can support private education could get ahead by learning in the public schools, maki ng something of 
their lives, and their families, and realizing what we call “the American dream”.   
 
So the State's lack of support for public education I find distressing.  We know and we've discussed t his numerous times 
before but the New Hampshire Supreme Court has rule d over and over again that the State of New Hampshi re is not 
coming even close to satisfying its constitutional obligation under the New Hampshire Constitution to provide an 
adequate - and even that's a low bar - but an adequate education for our children.  This, of course, occ urs at the same 
time when we see the legislature has abolished many  sources of revenue that have benefited and those p olicies have 
benefited more affluent residents and big corporations.  The cutting of the business taxes over time, the elimination of the 
business profits tax.  When the decision came shoul d we reduce property taxes and help with that or should we make 
these changes that benefit kind of a select few?  The choice has been to not to support public education and not to help 
property taxpayers across the State.
Board of Aldermen                                           10-13-2026                        Page 2 
 
And I wanted to mention in addition as part of this that as we see the voucher program growing like by unbelievable 
leaps and bounds, it is up 600% in five years to the point where now it is $64 million and in the curre nt fiscal year is the 
projected amount, and it's I'm sure going to keep growing.  Instead that, in my opinion, that money sho uld be directed 
into the public schools.  We see property taxes skyrocketing across the State because of school costs, which also are 
going up very quickly.  Special ed costs, transportation - these things are going up way more than the rate of inflation and 
at the same time, the State is reducing education aid for Nashua and many other cities and towns acros s New 
Hampshire.  So I wanted to let the Board know that there is going to be a $2 million problem.  Of course , we'll cover it 
with property taxes but an additional $2 million reduction by the State of New Hampshire.  
 
And finally Madam President, I wanted to mention that on Monday, October 26 th , we're going to have City Hall Trick or 
Treat.  I think it starts at around 3:30 and goes to 5.  Children from all over Nashua can come to City Hall to the various 
departments and can do Trick or Treat, you know, receive their little treats, candy and the like.  Our City employees do 
this every year and they I know they do a really good job in decorating and in handing out treats to the kids.  Actually, it's 
3:00 to 5:00 p.m. and this is on Monday, October 26th, which is Halloween week.  So we hope that as man y kids as 
possible can come to City Hall and enjoy that particular Halloween event.  And that's all I have, Madam President. 
 
President Wilshire 
 
Thank you, Mayor.   
 
RESPONSE TO REMARKS OF THE MAYOR  
  
Alderman Thibeault 
 
Thank you, Madam President.  Yeah, people continue to think there's a myth in this City that the downshifting is not 
affecting us in Nashua but we are last in school education being supported by the State.  That's 50 th  and we have a 
Governor that lives literally in this City and doesn't help support public education.  Her kids went to private.  I'm sure the 
Governor before that went to private.  They just don't care.  It's disgusting and it's sick because what's going to happen is 
we're going to cut programs.  That's what's going to happen, and we're going to cut teachers, and we're going to cut 
schools.  Maybe cutting schools is okay.  Cutting programs is not and that's what's going to happen.  Our taxes are going 
to go up and things are going to get cut that people are used to having.  People have to go and vote f or the right choices 
and make sure that we save public education because  it's going in the wrong direction and kids who need  - there's other 
cities and towns in the State where they've cut sports programs, and art programs, and music programs.  I f you don't 
play sports, you want other programs whether it's m usic, or art, or something else that you can go to, and if we have to 
cut those programs - Superintendent Andrade said it when I said, “If we cut $2 million out of this budget, what happens?” 
First thing he said is cut programs because you can't cut a school like this and you can't cut teachers like this when 
you've already had the contract out, right?  So first thing that would be cut is programs and that wou ld hurt our students. 
So I don't see why people still think the City's at fault here when we clearly have the facts that it's coming from up in the 
State.  Thank you.  
 
Alderman O’Brien 
 
Thank you, Madam President.  As some of you know, I  spent 16 years up there in Concord.  Some of those 16 years 
have been very shameful to me of the way the City of Nashua has been treated.  This example of educati on is the prime 
example.  I would like to turn the tune to something a little bit more radical because the majority of  the House is - call it 
for what it actually is – Republican - and these people evidently don't have a care.  I'm not saying all Republicans don't 
have a care for education but they look disdainfull y to citizens of Nashua, Manchester, Salem, our larger communities. 
They're more worried about having their view of the mountains up there in Bartlett.  They never supported us with 
projects that would benefit our City, that probably would help out in this situation and I'm talking about commuter rail.   
 
But now, they've added an extra $2 million to our taxpayers which is going to make us do some very seri ous cuts.  Are 
we going to potentially downsize the Police, the Fire Department, as well as education to make up the additional costs? 
Would it not be cheaper and entertain my thought - to probably deduct from what the State wants in taxes $4 million.  Let 
them sue us and tell them why we're doing it because we are committed by our Charter and by all rules in the State 
Constitution to educate our young and we're doing a good job of it except we're getting blindsided, hit in the back to 
which any football rep would have thrown the flag, but there's nobody up in Concord to throw the flag.  So we're 
independent.  We're on our own.  Maybe we should col laborate with our friends in Manchester.  Look at some radical 
means taking them to court.  Mr. Bolton are you busy?  
 
Steve Bolton, Corporation Counsel
Board of Aldermen                                           10-13-2026                        Page 3 
 
We have taken them to court.  
 
Alderman O’Brien 
 
Oh, I understand that.  You know, and Corporate Counsel what you say is true and you’re doing a fine job, but it falls on 
deaf ears.  The Republicans have been in charge of t he House for many, many, many years.  I saw even an ex-
Alderman come up to the State and hit one of the local State Representatives to write a Bill to institute the spending cap 
and you know who voted?  People from Bartlett, Lancaster, everybody else.  But all 28 Reps from the City of Nashua 
voted against it but it fell upon deaf ears because of the skewed numbers up there at the State House a nd I'm trying to 
wonder why does somebody from Bartlett or wherever (inaudible) or somewhere up there.  What gives them  the right to 
affect my sovereignty as a Nashua resident on how we  choose?  So maybe it's time.   
 
I know we've hit the seawall legally but they're not going to know that we're, you know, we can either be pacifists with this 
and roll over and let them – okay - you know, the State rub our belly or we can turn around and nip them.  It's just like 
something needs to be done and $4 million is no chump change, and that's going to come out of our taxpa yers, and I 
hope elections are coming.  That's our way to rectify things and I hope people do some soul searching a nd see what's 
happening up there.  I'm not saying we get great representation. There's 400 Reps that only get $100 a year.  For 16 
years, it actually cost me more money to be State Rep than I was actually making.  Since I'm no longer a State Rep, I 
had to go out and get a paper route to make some extra money.  But the thing is this is ridiculous, and a ridiculous 
system, and now it's affecting us.  
 
Let's look at some of the things that they have done.  Charter schools are public schools.  We bus the kids.  They're 
coming up with vouchers.  This is getting way, way, way, way too much.  My parents sent me to parochial  school 
because that was our Irish/Catholic faith, you know, and they made the sacrifices to do that.  If your kid wants to go to a 
charter school, so be it but fund it yourself.  That was always a choice.  If you can't fund it, we do supply an excellent, an 
excellent educational program.  Is the State blind that we do not have kids that go to Nashua High and Nashua South 
that don't go to Harvard?  They do.  We supply good education in the City.  The only one that's strangling us is the State 
of New Hampshire.  What happened to “Live Free and D ie?  Thank you, Madam President. 
 
Alderman Johnson 
 
Thank you.  I spent two years up at the State House and I couldn't wait to get out.  I'll tell you and I was on your side of 
the aisle.  So, ha, ha because I'll tell you, it was Alderman Clemons' mother and Betty Lasky who aske d me to run and 
he has a wonderful mother.  You know, great father, great family he comes from.  
 
But I just want to give a little bit of history and maybe Madam Chairman you can make sure I'm correct  here because 
when I was on the Board here, we used to get windfalls from the State.  We used to get $30, $40, $50 m illion dollars.  
We used to get quite a bit of money and the poorer towns didn't get it but we got it under Bernie Stre eter and I remember 
that.  In our education, we were flourishing but I guess things then changed.  But when I was in the S tate House, I also 
said we've never identified or came up with the meaning of what is an adequate education for kids.  So we're throwing 
mud against the wall because what is an adequate education?  We also heard from the School District that we’ll be short 
240 less free and reduced lunches and about 210 less children.  So that's going to affect it anyway because if you have 
less kids in the system, the State isn't going to pay you as much if you don't have as many kids in the system.  
 
The School District also told us that they were short.  We had to give them $150,000 because they were  short in the 
lunch program, which was self-sustaining all along.  Then when you listened to them, they said, "Well, part of it is 
because we gave them benefits”.  Well you can't give something if you don't have the money, and then i t's going to put 
you in the red, and you shouldn't be in the red.  I mean as a School District.  So the School District also has to make a lot 
of tough decisions that we can't make for them and I understand we're going to be short money.  But on  the other hand if 
your population is decreasing - like in any business, if your business is losing money, you have to mak e adjustments 
somewhere so you don't go belly up and the School Di strict could go belly up.  The State could take them over but you 
know what, they have to make tough decisions and you  can't always blame everything on the State because  if they 
made a bad choice and gave benefits that cost their lunch program not to be able to support itself anymore, that's not the 
State’s fault.  So I mean we can blame a lot on the State but we can also blame a lot here on fiscally  responsibility that 
people have to own up if they're not making the right choices within the District.  Thank you very muc h.

Laurie Ortolano 
 
Laurie Ortolano, Nashua.  I'm not going to rehash.  I came out to the Alderman hearing on the spending o f these 
Resolutions and the bonding of money, and I participated in that, and there's no reason for me to have to rehash that 
here.  But I would like to say that all of the Resolutions that are $2.5 million or less, I would have liked to have seen the 
language change to say they'll either be bonded or surplus money will be used to pay for them based on  what is left at 
the end of the year or by Q3.  I don't think these bonds will be sold by the end of the year and I think that we should see 
what's left.  We always do Christmas shopping in June where we come in and have $20 million and we say , "Oh, there's 
all these projects we didn't budget for and now we're going to go do them because we have surplus”.  No  more 
Christmas shopping in June.  Take that money and pay down bonds that you're taking out that don't meet the objective of 
the Ad Hoc Committee.  
 
Director Cummings made a very interesting statement in that meeting.  He said that the reason you're bonding the million 
dollars or two is because it takes time to implement that program.  What does that mean?  It's on the third year.  How 
much time does it take?  There was no explanation given.  Somebody in this chamber should ask Director Cummings 
what does that mean?  When is the time going to be right that you have money that you don't have to bo nd a million, 
$1.5, $2 million, $2.5.  Pay it down out of surplus and put the option in the Resolution.   
 
Also, I'd like to speak to the walking or the disabilities Zoom meeting ordinance.  You know, I've expressed my concerns 
about that.  I am really concerned that the sponsor of that is being hung out to dry by the Legal offic e by not getting the 
right interpretation of reading.  Now, Alderman Kelly did not vote on that in Personnel/Administrative Affairs because she 
wanted the input of Legal.  She's not here.  So the very reasons why we didn't get a vote is because s he was coming
